blocks.content: This topic covers the real, fundamental distinction between declarative and imperative approaches, already introduced briefly in the Infrastructure as Code topic.
1. Declarative, Defined
Declarative genuinely means describing the desired, real end state, what you want infrastructure to look like, without specifying the exact, real steps.
Terraform, already covered, is genuinely, fully declarative, every configuration file describes an end state, not a genuine, real sequence of actions.
This real, foundational distinction shapes everything about how Terraform configurations are genuinely written, read, and reasoned about, throughout this course.
By the end of this topic, this real distinction should feel clear enough to genuinely recognize in any, new tool encountered, beyond this course.

blocks.content: 2. Imperative, Defined
Imperative genuinely means describing the exact, real steps to reach a goal, first do this, then do that, in a specific, real, defined order.
A real, imperative shell script explicitly lists each, individual command, in the genuine, exact sequence it must actually, really run.
This real contrast with declarative, already covered, is worth holding in mind directly, together they form this topic's entire, core, real distinction.
Recognizing imperative code when encountered elsewhere sharpens appreciation for what Terraform's genuinely declarative approach actually, practically saves you.

blocks.content: 3. A Real, Side-by-Side Example
A real, side-by-side example, provisioning one server, makes this distinction genuinely concrete, declarative code versus an imperative, step-by-step script.
The real declarative version simply states the desired server, the real imperative version explicitly lists each, individual, real provisioning command.
This real, concrete comparison is worth studying directly, abstract definitions matter less than seeing this, genuine distinction in real, actual code.
This connects directly back to the real, side-by-side comparison already covered in the Infrastructure as Code topic, applied here more, precisely.

# Declarative (Terraform):
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = "ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
}

# Imperative (a real shell script):
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0 --instance-type t3.micro

Terraform is genuinely, fully declarative, you describe what you genuinely want, the desired, real end state, not the real, specific how to get there.

blocks.content: 5. Real Idempotency
Real idempotency means applying the exact, same, declarative configuration twice genuinely changes nothing the second, real time, nothing new happens.
This real property is a direct, genuine consequence of being declarative, an imperative script, run twice, often genuinely, actually causes real problems.
This connects directly back to real, genuine consistency, already covered in the Why Terraform and Benefits of IaC topics, idempotency is its real mechanism.
This real, powerful property is worth testing directly, running terraform apply twice in a genuine row, and observing no, further, real changes occur.

blocks.content: 9. A Real, Common Mistake
Thinking in steps, while genuinely writing declarative code, is a real, common mistake, especially for someone new, coming from a genuinely imperative background.
